entries.note: Means a span or period; its Proto-Indo-European root means to divide. It replaced [[tide]], and the hosts contrast it with Latin [[tempus]], meaning to stretch.
Old English word for [[time]] in general, not just the sea's movement; it also meant an hour before French [[hour]] was imported.
Latin word for time, said to mean to stretch; the hosts contrast it with the Germanic idea of [[time]] as a division.
Imitates the tick-like sound of an early square sheet-metal bell; adopted in the 14th century, probably from medieval Latin, possibly Celtic, and resembles German [[Glocke|Glocken]].
Old English word for a timepiece used before [[clock]] arrived in the 14th century, literally a day measure.
Latin word for a timepiece, the source of [[horology]]; we still describe timepieces as horological.
Greek word for a water clock, literally water thief, sharing its stealing element with [[kleptomaniac]]; time was measured by water dripping into another vessel.
The wrist clock is named for us looking at it, whereas other languages, such as French [[montre]], name it for showing the time.
French word for a [[watch]], meaning show, because the device shows the time.
Means the thing opposite or facing you, which is why a clock or watch has a face that looks at us.
Same word as ordinal second, from Latin [[secunda minuta]], a second reduction of the hour. Before the Normans brought it, English used [[other]] instead.
The same word as minute meaning tiny: the small parts of an hour, the [[minuta prima|first minutes]]. The original medieval minute was a tenth of an hour.
From Greek hora, a unit or interval; the H was never pronounced in English, French or Spanish, though it is in [[horology]]. It shares an ancient root with [[year]].
A very old Germanic word, probably from the same root as the Greek source of [[hour]]; the root meant both year and season.
In the medieval system Bartholomeus Anglicus described (also mentioned by Bede), a quarter of an hour, made up of ten [[moment|moments]]; also called a [[prick]].
A medieval unit of time: a tenth of a [[point]], made up of twelve [[ounce|ounces]].
A medieval unit of time: a twelfth of a [[moment]], made up of 47 [[atom|atoms]].
The smallest medieval time unit, meaning something that can't be divided: 22,560 per hour, far too small to measure then. It is unrelated to atomic clocks.
Another medieval name for the time unit called a [[point]], which Rob finds juvenilely funny; English literature has many prick-and-point jokes.
From a Proto-Germanic root meaning to burn or be hot, likely from a heat-related Proto-Indo-European root. It is related to a Sanskrit word for a glow in the sky.
The same word as dusky, meaning the darkest part of the day that isn't night; Old English dox underwent metathesis, like [[ask]] and axe.
From Latin nona, the ninth hour counted from 6 a.m., so originally about 3 p.m. It later moved to midday, giving [[afternoon]] and [[forenoon]].
Began as references to after [[noon]] that fused into a single word, alongside [[forenoon]].
Began as before [[noon]], became a word for the morning, and has now largely fallen out of use.
Light that comes between, when the sun is below the horizon; originally it referred to both morning and evening, not just the end of the day.
From the Latin word for twilight or dusk; it describes twilight hours and species that are active at twilight.
Called a Shakespeare coinage, clipped from the earlier [[dawning]], perhaps to fit his pentameter; also mentioned in the Shakespeare episode.
The name for a ten-day week in the French Revolutionary calendar, where each 30-day month had three; it meant ten days, not ten years.
In German (and other Germanic languages) half one means 12:30, halfway to one, whereas in British English it means 1:30, which causes missed meetings.
A joke in the Philippines that Filipino time means being late; many cultures joke similarly, for example about [[Indian Standard Time]].
Jokingly said by Jess's Indian friends to mean showing up an hour late, like [[Filipino time]].
Literally a turning or succession, sharing a root with [[vice versa]] and [[vicarious]]; perhaps originally a change of duty, a theory backed by Old Icelandic [[vika]].
Odin's day, with Odin called Woden by the Anglo-Saxons; a Germanic translation of the Roman planetary day names, covered in the mythology episode.
Thor's day, one of the Germanic translations of the Roman planetary day names.
Old Icelandic for a distance traveled at sea, perhaps how far you rowed before changing rowers; it supports the change-of-duty theory for [[week]].
Moon day; the moon is named in both Monday and every [[month]].
Named after Tiw, the Germanic god of war.
Jess suggests Freya's day, but Rob says it is generally thought to be Frigg's day; the two goddesses are similar but not identical.
Named for Saturn, a return to Latin among the otherwise Germanic day names.
Named for the sun.
From Latin calendarium, an account book or register; originally a debt register, because interest was due on the [[kalends]].
The first day of the Roman month, from [[calare]] meaning to call out, because priests publicly proclaimed it after observing the new moon.
Germanic, but from the same Proto-Indo-European root as Latin [[calare]], and it also meant to call out.
Literally the sun standing still; knowing this helps Rob tell it apart from [[equinox]].
Literally equal night, one of the transparent calendar terms along with [[solstice]].
A unit of two weeks, from Old English for fourteen nights; common in Britain but rarely used in the US; its counterpart was [[sennight]].
From Old English for seven nights, a unit of seven days and counterpart of [[fortnight]]; no longer used.
Used since Old English for a period of twelve months, distinct from the calendar [[year]]; it appears in the 1800s folk song All Around My Hat.
A lost English word for the day before yesterday; compare German [[vorgestern]]. The hosts want to revive it with [[overmorrow]].
A lost English word for the day after tomorrow, like German [[übermorgen]]; the hosts think it sounds modern and fun enough to revive.
German for the day after tomorrow, still in use, unlike English [[overmorrow]].
German for the day before yesterday; stacking more vors goes further back in time. Compare English [[ereyesterday]].
Basically means a measurement, related to [[meter]], [[dimension]], [[menstrual]], [[menopause]], [[semester]] and [[trimester]]; it roughly matches a lunar cycle, so the moon names it.
Means three months, not a division into three; Rob realized this during his wife's pregnancy. It is related to [[month]].
From Latin for six months, not half a year's worth of months; related to [[month]] and [[trimester]], though semesters no longer last six months.
Also called the Platonic year: the roughly 25,920 (now 25,800) years it takes Earth's tilting axis to return to its original position. The hosts don't know Plato's connection.
Essentially means a sowing; it was used more generally until the 14th century, when four fixed seasons were settled on.
Means to winterize yourself, and it evokes the French word for winter, [[hiver]].
The American name for the season, with a sense of decaying and dying; like [[autumn]], it replaced the older [[harvest]], and is unusual among Germanic languages.
The British name for the season, borrowed from French and said to mean increase; like [[fall]], it replaced the older [[harvest]].
The earlier English name for the season now called [[fall]] or [[autumn]]; many other Germanic languages still use their version of harvest.
One of the scarier Anglo-Saxon month names, covered in the earlier calendar episode.
The Anglo-Saxon month when cows were milked extra; like all Anglo-Saxon month names it ended in 'month', and was covered in the calendar episode.
